title: Special linear groups are reductive in every characteristic
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $r\geq1$, and let $E$ be an $r$-dimensional $k$-vector space. The special linear group scheme $G=\operatorname{SL}(E)$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], representing $R\mapsto\{g\in\operatorname{Aut}_R(E\otimes_kR):\det(g)=1\}$ on commutative $k$-algebras, is smooth, affine, of finite type, and geometrically connected (connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]). It is reductive: after extension to an algebraic closure it has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Here unipotent means that, in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation, all geometric points are matrices $u$ with $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N>0$. Smooth and finite type have the meanings in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; group schemes have the meaning in [def-sc-group-scheme]. No characteristic restriction is imposed.

source.place: Section 2.42, printed p.53 (smooth connected SL), Corollary 19.18 and Example 19.19, printed p.401 (standard faithful absolutely simple representation implies reductive); r=1 is the trivial group.

proof.text: Choose a basis of $E$. For every $k$-algebra $R$ it identifies $E\otimes_kR$ with $R^r$, with automorphisms and determinant given by their matrices. Thus [def-sc-general-linear-group] identifies $G$ with $\operatorname{Spec}C$, where $P=k[x_{ij}]$, $D=\det(x_{ij})$ and $C=P/(D-1)$, and supplies its group structure and inclusion $j:G\hookrightarrow H=\operatorname{GL}_{r,k}$. The $r^2$ residue classes generate $C$, so this single affine chart makes $G$ of finite type by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. The same presentation has finitely many variables and one relation, so $G$ is locally of finite presentation by [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. For $r=1$ it is $\operatorname{Spec}k[x]/(x-1)=\operatorname{Spec}k$.

source.place: Section 2.42, printed p.53; determinant-one coordinate presentation in section 2.a; finite presentation written explicitly.

proof.text: Write $B=P[1/D]$, the coordinate algebra of $H$. Define a ring map $q^*:C\to B$ by $\bar x_{i1}\mapsto D^{-1}x_{i1}$ and $\bar x_{ij}\mapsto x_{ij}$ for $j>1$. Each monomial in the determinant contains exactly one entry of the first column, so its value on these images is $D^{-1}D=1$; hence the relation $D-1$ maps to zero. Polynomial evaluation [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] and the quotient construction [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient] give this map. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum] it defines $q:H\to G$, with $q(g)=g\operatorname{diag}(\det(g)^{-1},1,\ldots,1)$. The map $j^*:B\to C$ sends $D^{-1}$ to $1$, so $j^*q^*$ fixes every generator of $C$. Thus $qj=\mathrm{id}_G$. This is a scheme retraction; it need not be a group homomorphism.

source.place: Section 2.42, printed p.53: inverse to (A,t) ↦ A diag(t,1,...,1), followed by projection to SL.

proof.text: The group $H$ is smooth by [lem-sfb-general-linear-reductive]. Let $T\subset T'$ be any first order thickening of affine $k$-schemes and $a:T\to G$ any $k$-morphism. By smoothness of $H$, in the lifting definition of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], $ja:T\to H$ extends to a $k$-morphism $b:T'\to H$. Then $qb:T'\to G$ restricts to $qja=a$. Hence $G$ is formally smooth; together with its finite presentation from step 1, the same definition proves smoothness. This explicitly supplies every required lift, rather than invoking a new descent or retract theorem.

source.place: Section 2.42, printed p.53: scheme retraction; formal-smoothness lifting argument expanded using Stacks Tag 02H0 (more-morphisms, definition-formally-smooth).

proof.text: Let $K=\bar k$. Base change preserves the equality $qj=\mathrm{id}_G$, so $q_K:H_K\to G_K$ is surjective on the underlying spaces. The geometric connectedness clause of [lem-sfb-general-linear-reductive] says that $H_K$ is connected. If $G_K=A\amalg A'$ were a partition into two nonempty open-and-closed subsets, their inverse images under the continuous map $q_K$ would also be disjoint open-and-closed subsets covering $H_K$, and both would be nonempty by surjectivity. This contradicts [def-weil-connected-scheme]. The identity section gives a point of $G_K$, so it is nonempty. Thus $G_K$ is connected, which is the asserted geometric connectedness.

source.place: Section 2.42, printed p.53: connectedness from the GL ≅ SL × G_m decomposition; the continuous-image argument is written out.

proof.text: For the remaining argument identify $G_K$ with $\operatorname{SL}_{r,K}$ at the level of schemes. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] its coordinate ring is $C\otimes_kK$. Set $C_K=K[x_{ij}]/(D-1)$. Send $(\bar f)\otimes a$ to $a\bar f$ in $C_K$, using [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. In the other direction send $a\in K$ to $1\otimes a$ and $x_{ij}$ to $\bar x_{ij}\otimes1$. Polynomial evaluation and the quotient relation give this map, since the determinant of the latter matrix is $1\otimes1$. Both composites fix the coefficients and every variable and hence are the identity. These maps also preserve multiplication of matrices, identity and inverse: the coordinate formulas in [def-sc-general-linear-group] are finite sums, products and signed minors with integer coefficients. Thus this is an identification of group schemes as well as coordinate rings.

source.place: Section 2.42 and Corollary 19.18: extension to an algebraic closure; explicit coordinate-algebra base change.

proof.text: Let $U\hookrightarrow G_K$ be any smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup scheme. By the affine closed-immersion criterion of [def-weil-closed-immersion], $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $C_K\twoheadrightarrow A$; hence $A$ is a finitely generated $K$-algebra. The inclusion into $G_K\subset\operatorname{GL}_{r,K}$ is a rational representation on $K^r$. The unipotence hypothesis provides some faithful matrix representation of $U$ whose geometric points are unipotent; it is not necessary to assume this for the inclusion representation. Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-rational-representation-fixed-vector]: $K$ is algebraically closed, $U$ is smooth, affine and of finite type, its given representation is faithful on all algebra-points, and $r\geq1$. Therefore the subspace $W=\{v\in K^r:uv=v\text{ for all }u\in U(K)\}$ contains a nonzero vector.

source.place: Lemma 19.16, Corollary 19.18 and Example 19.19, printed p.401; Proposition 14.3, p.280, and Corollary 14.12, p.283 (fixed vectors from the matrix criterion).

proof.text:
Normality [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] implies $g^{-1}ug\in U(K)$ for $g\in\operatorname{SL}_r(K)$, $u\in U(K)$. Consequently $u(gw)=g(g^{-1}ug)w=gw$ for $w\in W$, so $W$ is stable under $\operatorname{SL}_r(K)$. Choose $w\in W$ with $w_j
e0$. If $r=1$, then $W=K^1$. If $r>1$, choose $i
e j$. The transvection $T_{ij}=I+E_{ij}$ has determinant $1$ (adding one row of the identity to a different row leaves its determinant unchanged) and inverse $I-E_{ij}$. Thus $T_{ij}w-w=w_je_i\in W$ and $e_i\in W$. For every $a
e i$, the determinant-one transvection $T_{ai}$ gives $T_{ai}e_i-e_i=e_a\in W$. All basis vectors belong to $W$, so $W=K^r$. Hence every $u\in U(K)$ has identity matrix. This calculation also works in characteristic $2$; no division by $r$, a characteristic, or a difference of field elements is used.

source.place: Lemma 19.16 and Example 19.19, printed p.401: normality preserves invariants and the standard SL representation is simple; explicit transvection proof.

proof.text: By [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], applied to $U\to\operatorname{Spec}K$, its coordinate algebra $A$ is reduced. It is finitely generated by step 6. Each image $a_{ij}$ of $x_{ij}-\delta_{ij}$ in $A$ vanishes at every $K$-point by step 7. Clause 2 of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] gives $a_{ij}=0$. The surjection $C_K\twoheadrightarrow A$ thus sends every variable to its identity-matrix scalar, and therefore $K\to A$ is surjective. The identity section of $U$ supplies a retraction $A\to K$, so $K\to A$ is also injective. Thus $A\cong K$ and $U$ is the trivial subgroup scheme, not merely a subgroup with trivial $K$-points. This proves reductivity. Together with steps 1, 3 and 4 it gives all the asserted properties of $\operatorname{SL}(E)$.

source.place: Lemma 19.16 and Corollary 19.18, printed p.401; scheme-theoretic triviality expanded by Stacks Tag 056T (varieties, lemma-smooth-geometrically-normal) and affine Nullstellensatz.
